newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Ford makes tentative deal with Canada union.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ford makes tentative deal with Canada union.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. of Canada Ltd. and the Canadian Auto Workers union reached a tentative contract agreement on Wednesday, seven hours ahead of a 7 P.M. EST/ 2400 GMT strike deadline, the union said.
"As of noon today, we have informed Mr. (Ford chief negotiator Donald) McKenzie that we have a tentative agreement," CAW President Buzz Hargrove told a news conference.

The tentative three-year deal with Ford's Canadian unit ends the 1996 bargaining season for Canada's big three automakers and follows the pattern agreement forged at Chrysler Corp's Canadian unit in September and at General Motors Corp.'s Canada unit in October after a 20-day strike.

Hargrove told reporters the union's master committee unanimously recommended the deal to the Ford membership and would hold a ratification vote on Saturday and Sunday. The results will be released Sunday night.
Ford's McKenzie said the carmaker's executives were pleased with the deal and that "it happened as far ahead of the deadline as it did."
Hargrove had said on Tuesday he thought the deal could be concluded that night. But the agreement was held up by issues such as the right to refuse unsafe work, and same-sex benefits.

The pattern deal offers the union protection from outsourcing, or contracting out jobs, ensures minimum health and safety and employment standards and gives workers improved benefits and a 10.2 percent wage and cost of living increase over three years.
Hargrove said the provisions restricting outsourcing would be a big part of the union's bargaining position for workers it represents in other industries.
The Ford deal includes a ban on the sale or closing of all Ford plants in Canada, except Ford's Windsor, Ontario engine plant, which is being closed this month.
The union said Ford agreed to buy out some of the 600 workers at the engine plant and shift others to Ford's remaining Windsor plants.
Hargrove said the Ford negotiations were not as difficult as those at Chrysler or GM.
An unidentified Ford executive said Ford Canada accepted the pattern agreement more readily than Chrysler or GM because Ford decided it had an "obligation to its employees" in Canada.
But analysts said it was difficult for Ford to break from the pattern since it was the last of the three carmakers to bargain with the union.
"Once you are in the position of being last up, you are caught," said Denis Desrosier, president of DesRosier Automotive Consultants Inc.
